item.title: Small counties, big appeal: China's "golden week" fuels diverse getaways
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
*During this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips, averaging 300 million a day.
*Cultural and tourism authorities nationwide have introduced a range of creative initiatives to attract visitors, drawing on sports events, cultural IPs, ethnic traditions and distinctive natural landscapes.
*On Sept. 24, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced plans to develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life during 2026-2030, aimed at helping foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays and gain a closer view of contemporary China.
BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- While tourism in China has traditionally been associated with breathtaking landscapes and photo opportunities, Wang Xin (pseudonym) opted for a different kind of National Day holiday this year: watching tennis.
Well before the vacation she had purchased tickets for the Jingshan Tennis Open in central China's Hubei Province.
A resident of Dongguan in Guangdong Province, about 1,000 kilometers away, she first learned about Jingshan because of the tournament. "I want to watch matches featuring several young WTA (Women's Tennis Association) and ATP (Association of Tennis Professionals) players up close," said the tennis enthusiast.
She planned to spend three days watching the matches and the remaining four days exploring the county-level city, taking in its scenic mountains, valleys, and forests.
During this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, one of China's few annual "golden weeks," authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips, averaging 300 million a day.
People enjoy a match during the Jingshan Tennis Open in Jingshan, central China's Hubei Province, Oct. 4, 2026. (Photo by Lei Yixin/Xinhua)
Data from Meituan, a major services platform, showed homestay bookings for four-to-six-night stays during the holiday rose 24 percent year on year as of Sept. 28, with county-level destinations posting particularly strong growth.
DESTINATIONS FOR DIVERSE DEMANDS
Jingshan, a county-level city where tennis has been developing for more than 40 years, is known as China's "hometown of tennis."
To boost tourism during the National Day holiday, local authorities announced that during the tournament period, a match ticket would entitle holders to discounts at over 100 local businesses. Merchants have also benefited from the holiday travel surge.
Zuo Meng, a vendor selling knitted products, said she follows the local tennis events closely. "In Jingshan, there are tennis matches almost every week," she said, adding that a tournament can generate 6,000 to 7,000 yuan (about 895 to 1,044 U.S. dollars) in sales. Over the past two years, she has also taught knitting skills to more than 200 women so they, too, could benefit from tourism.
Peng Jufang runs a farm in Wenfeng Village. Noticing tourists' enthusiasm for tennis, he founded his own tennis club in October last year. With more than 16 people coming each day to try their hand at tennis, he was kept busy during this National Day holiday, teaching visitors for over six hours a day.
In 2025, Jingshan hosted 48 domestic and international sports events. The comprehensive output value of its "tennis plus" economy surpassed 3.5 billion yuan, drawing 3.52 million visits for matches and tourism.
While Wang Xin enjoys tennis matches in Jingshan, cultural enthusiasts have meccas of their own to visit.
Wang Yinan, in her 20s, traveled from Beijing to Ruicheng County in north China's Shanxi Province after watching the popular animation "All Wishes Come True." Hometown of the legendary figure behind the film's main protagonist, Lyu Dongbin, Ruicheng is home to the Yongle Palace, which is known for its celebrated murals.
"It is such an exciting trip, and it's incredible to be in Lyu's hometown," said Wang, as she browsed creative products at the Yongle Palace store.
Visitors are seen during a study tour for mural copying at the Yongle Palace scenic area in Ruicheng, north China's Shanxi Province, Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Guo Song/Xinhua)
Liu Haibo, chairman of the Yongle Cultural Tourism Investment and Construction Co., Ltd., said the scenic site rolled out customized services to sustain its tourism growth following its viral popularity. Visitors can take photos in dedicated photo zones, guides explain the murals by linking them to scenes from the film, and tourists can attend interactive classes to learn mural copying and line drawing.
The movie has helped raise the profile of Ruicheng, making it a sought-after destination, especially among young people. Statistics showed that between Oct. 1 and 5, Yongle Palace received about 80,000 visits, up more than 50 percent year on year.
The ancient township of Fenghuang in Xiangxi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, central China's Hunan Province, has kept its tourist momentum following the Sept. 25-27 Mid-Autumn Festival holiday.
During the National Day holiday, some visitors seeking to avoid the crowds have ventured beyond the ancient town of Fenghuang into surrounding mountains and villages, exploring rich ethnic cultures, such as Miao welcoming rituals, lantern shows and folk performances.
INTERNATIONAL VISITORS JOINING THE RUSH
The diverse tourism resources in China's counties are also luring international visitors away from metropolises like Beijing and Shanghai and toward niche attractions.
Lucas Martin, 28, from France, visited Fenghuang for the first time after touring major Chinese cities.
"Fenghuang feels entirely different from big cities," he said. "You can slow down here. You can admire the distinctive stilt houses lining the Tuojiang River and observe local residents in their daily lives."
The in-depth county exploration impressed him with the town's authentic living vibe. "This is not merely a tourist attraction. Walking along the river and pausing at street corners makes me feel more than just a passing sightseer."
Foreign tourists try specialty food of the Miao ethnic group at the ancient township of Fenghuang in Xiangxi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, central China's Hunan Province, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Hu Cong/Xinhua)
Emma Wilson, an Australian traveler who is exploring small towns and countryside across China, tried on Miao ceremonial costumes in Fenghuang.
"It is magical to walk into the old streets, dressed like locals," she said. Shop staff carefully helped her get fitted in the ethnic costume.
"A simple landscape photo fades quickly from memory. But putting on traditional clothing, tasting local food and learning the stories behind folk customs create experiences that stay with you far longer," she said.
Since December 2023, when China launched a trial policy granting unilateral visa exemptions to visitors from six countries, it has expanded unilateral visa-free entry to travelers from 50 countries as of September, allowing eligible visitors to stay for up to 30 days.
In a separate move, authorities extended the visa-free transit period for certain countries from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours in December 2024. So far the number of eligible countries has increased to 57.
Official data revealed that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the first eight months of 2026, up 19.5 percent year on year, while one of the leading mobile payment platforms, Weixin Pay, reported that both the value and number of e-wallet transactions made by overseas users rose by more than 80 percent during the same period.
On Sept. 24, China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced plans to develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life during 2026-2030, aimed at helping foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays and gain a closer view of contemporary China.
A National Day gala is held on the Tuojiang River at the ancient township of Fenghuang in Xiangxi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, central China's Hunan Province, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Hu Cong/Xinhua)
FROM "CITY WALK" TO "COUNTRY WALK"
Yang Han, a researcher at an institute affiliated to the travel platform Qunar, believes that county-level tourism began to accelerate around 2023-2024, as travelers increasingly sought destinations with fewer crowds, a lively atmosphere, opportunities for relaxation and immersive local experiences, as well as greater value for money.
For instance, in Ruicheng of Shanxi, a set meal for one person may cost less than 20 yuan, the price of a cup of bubble tea in Beijing.
Tuo Yanzheng, a professor at the College of Tourism and Service Management, Nankai University, said county areas hold rich agricultural, ecological and cultural resources with untapped consumption potential.
"The key lies in turning these resource strengths into distinctive tourism products and consumption scenarios," she said. "It can not only meet people's increasingly diverse consumption demands, but also inject new vitality into the county economy."
According to Sun Jiashan, a researcher at the Central Institute of Socialism, China's tourism market has evolved from "City Walk" to "Country Walk."
Steadily improving transportation has made county-level destinations more accessible. By the end of 2025, China's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
Shortly before the National Day holiday, the country opened four major high-speed railway sections, improving transport links across several regions and making travel easier for residents. The high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, with eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines.
In addition, Sun noted that beyond scenic spots, historical sites and natural landscapes, tourists are increasingly drawn to vibrant scenes of everyday life, such as farmers' markets and bustling streets. "This shift also places higher demands on local cultural and tourism infrastructure and services," he said.
"As overseas tourists venture beyond first-tier cities into central and western regions and county-level areas, they encounter not only the outward face of China's development but also the texture of everyday social life," he said. "This helps break through cognitive filters and information barriers in Western societies and presents a real China to the world."

item.title: Culture-infused tourism gains traction during National Day holiday
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
Tourists pose for a photo at the Hetou Old Street scenic area in Fengnan District of Tangshan City, north China's Hebei Province, Oct. 3, 2026. (Photo by Li Xiuqing/Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- On the morning of Oct. 1, the first day of China's National Day holiday, the Confucius cruise ship slowly pulled away from a port in Jining, east China's Shandong Province, setting off for Nanyang ancient town on the city's southern outskirts.
Named after the famous ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius, the ship was bound for a 2-hour-plus journey, passing stretches of the Grand Canal, the world's oldest artificial waterway system, which connects rivers in northern and eastern China and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014.
"We chose the cruise after seeing online that it offered a rich cultural experience," said Zhao Xiaojie from the provincial capital Jinan, as she and her 11-year-old son read the ancient texts on the cabin's decorations inspired by the Six Arts -- the six foundational disciplines of ancient Confucian education.
Her choice reflects a broader trend during this year's National Day holiday, as cultural content is weighing more and more heavily in China's tourism products.
NATIONAL DAY EXTRAVAGANZA
"Cruises have operated on the same route before, but the Confucius incorporates many cultural elements and intangible cultural heritage experiences, turning it into a moving showcase of Confucianism on the Grand Canal," said Zhang Feng, head of the cruise route.
The round-trip ticket includes shuttle services to scenic spots and admission to the Kangqian Bieyuan and Huji Qianzhuang attractions. Visitors can also watch a traditional fishermen's wedding ceremony and cormorant fishing performances in Nanyang ancient town, Zhang said.
Such packages bring together Confucianism and the culture of the Grand Canal, he added.
The unusual holiday calendar this year, with the Mid-Autumn Festival falling just three working days before the National Day holiday, has given fresh momentum to the integration of culture and tourism.
Data from Chinese online travel platform Ctrip showed that one in 10 travelers chose to combine the two holidays by taking three days off to create a 13-day break. Nearly half of those taking an extended break traveled for more than eight days.
The longer holidays have expanded the travel radius of Chinese tourists, bringing cultural and tourism products in more remote and lesser-known destinations into the spotlight.
In Cangyuan Wa Autonomous County, southwest China's Yunnan Province, for example, tourists gathered at a square to pound freshly harvested rice and prepare new rice, filling the air with its aroma.
"New rice festival activities and service facilities have been upgraded this year, allowing visitors to experience the authentic culture of the Wa ethnic group," said Li Lei, deputy general manager of the Cangyuan County Tourism Investment Company.
Traditional culture is not the only draw. A growing number of travelers are also visiting landmarks associated with China's revolutionary history, driven in part by the patriotic sentiment associated with the National Day holiday.
This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which lasted from 1934 to 1936. The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
In Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province, the Memorial Park of the Starting Point of the Central Red Army's Long March has attracted large numbers of study-tour groups and is expected to receive nearly 300,000 visits during the seven-day holiday.
Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said the flow of visitors to revolutionary landmarks reflects people's emotional identification with the revolutionary traditions.
When they travel, they don't just want to see history; they also want to draw deeper inspiration from the revolutionary legacy for their lives today, according to him.
INNOVATION REMAINS KEY
The trend has also fallen in line with a series of development plans China released recently.
The 15th Five-Year Plan for culture and tourism development, released by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism in September, calls for deeper integration between culture and tourism and their mutually reinforcing development with other areas of the economy and society. It stresses supporting the development of distinctive cultural industries and tourism in former revolutionary base areas.
Moreover, it calls for expanding the space for cultural and tourism development, with deeper integration moving from resource consolidation and product integration toward new business models and broader applications.
Hong'an Township in Xiushan Tujia and Miao Autonomous County, southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, has put such innovation into practice, drawing 190,000 tourist visits in the first two days of the holiday.
Leveraging the cultural appeal of Border Town, a novel by renowned Chinese writer Shen Congwen, as well as its unique location where three provincial-level regions meet, the township has developed immersive, scenario-based tourism offerings that combine folk experiences, local cuisine and the nighttime economy.
In Shandong, seven cities have joined forces to combine seven popular online-literature IPs with the region's landscapes and historical sites, encouraging fans to turn fictional worlds into real-life travel destinations.
The model uses storytelling familiar to Generation Z to breathe new life into traditional cultural and tourism resources, converting online popularity into real-world tourism consumption.
"The route runs from west to east, so fans can take a high-speed train and visit a different 'chapter' every day, which is very convenient," said Liu Wei, a fan of online literature born in the 2000s.
For industry insiders, such efforts to generate more immersive cultural tourist activities are also necessary.
Wu Liyun, a professor at Beijing International Studies University, said scenic spots once relied mainly on ticket sales, which is often unsustainable today.
"The core of the industry transformation lies in adding more experiential offerings and opportunities for secondary consumption, with the focus on everyday settings, local culture and lifestyle-oriented services," she said.
GLOBAL DRAW
The shift has appealed to inbound travelers as well.
With China offering unilateral visa-free entry to citizens of 50 countries and full mutual visa exemptions with 29 countries, its tourism industry has also been working to offer overseas tourists a wider range of immersive trips centered on cultural experiences.
In Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province, where the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in July, growing numbers of overseas visitors are exploring historic sites, taking part in art workshops and browsing handicraft markets, while enjoying distinctive cafes and homestays.
The city, known as the "Porcelain Capital," now offers a range of experiences for visitors seeking to explore its centuries-old ceramic traditions, according to Zhang Chen, a local tourism industry insider. Options include a one-day program combining an introduction to local ceramic culture with hands-on pottery making, or a three-day workshop led by inheritors of intangible cultural heritage.
"Many overseas visitors now seek a deeper cultural connection, rather than simply sightseeing," Zhang said.
In Beijing, veteran tourist guide Dou Junjie feels a similar trend. He provides guided bicycle tours along the Beijing Central Axis, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2024 that covers former imperial palaces and sacrificial structures.
"More overseas visitors to Beijing would like to experience local life and learn about local culture," Dou said.
According to Gao Zhengyang, a guest researcher with Jiangsu Su Merchants Bank, immersive travel across destinations is replacing sightseeing and photo stops, a wider range of trendy Chinese products is making its way onto tourists' shopping lists, and the mix of visitors is becoming more diverse. Gao said all of these trends point to improvements in the quality of "China Travel."
Data from Ctrip shows that bookings for one-day tours by inbound tourists during this year's National Day holiday and the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday surged by over 400 percent year on year, with scenic spot ticket sales up more than 220 percent and train tickets more than 170 percent.
Li Xinjian, a professor at the Beijing International Studies University, said the growth in inbound tourism during what is traditionally a peak season for domestic travel reflects the increasingly diverse experiences on offer.
"Overseas tourists are finding that China offers not only beautiful scenery but also engaging cultural experiences," he said.
For Wu Liyun, value-added services such as the cultural experiences in Jingdezhen and Beijing are particularly important, as they are far more appealing than standardized products and usually leave a much deeper impression on travelers.
Wu believes Jingdezhen's model can be replicated in terms of how cultural content is presented. She cited her hometown of Linyi in Shandong Province, where willow weaving products are widely exported, and tourists can try their hand at the traditional craft and take their own creations home.
"Every city has its own ways of life passed down through generations," she said. "What you are accustomed to in the place where you live can be incredibly fresh and novel to outsiders."

item.title: China's railways see holiday return peak amid vibrant tourism market
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
Passengers are seen at the waiting hall of Tianjin Railway Station in north China's Tianjin, Oct. 7, 2026. As the National Day holiday is drawing to a close, return travel flows increase across the country. (Photo by Du Penghui/Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's railways saw the peak of the holiday return rush on Wednesday, with 24.15 million passenger trips expected on the final day of the National Day holiday, amid strong travel demand and vibrant tourism activity across the country.
A total of 2,449 additional passenger trains were scheduled on Wednesday to cope with the surge in demand, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd.
On Tuesday, the country's railways handled 21.6 million passenger trips, marking the third consecutive day with more than 20 million journeys.
Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an, Wuhan, Hangzhou, Chongqing and Shanghai were among the busiest cities for departures and arrivals, while passenger flows were particularly heavy on routes including Beijing-Shanghai, Wuhan-Shanghai, Wuhan-Shenzhen and Xi'an-Chengdu.
Railway authorities across the country added services and expanded overnight operations to facilitate the return rush as China's tourism market remained vibrant during the seven-day holiday, with county-level destinations and nighttime consumption emerging as notable trends.
County-level destinations gained popularity as travelers increasingly sought slower-paced and more immersive experiences away from major cities.
From the coastal county of Lingshui in south China's Hainan Province to Mohe, a county-level city on the country's northern frontier, smaller destinations are drawing visitors with distinctive local experiences.
Meanwhile, nighttime consumption flourished in many cities, with cultural performances, night markets, light shows and food fairs extending visitor stays and enriching holiday experiences.
Passengers are seen at the waiting hall of Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station in east China's Shanghai, Oct. 7, 2026. As the National Day holiday is drawing to a close, return travel flows increase across the country. (Xinhua/Ding Ting)
Passengers are seen at the waiting hall of Wuhan Railway Station in Wuhan, central China's Hubei Province, Oct. 7, 2026. As the National Day holiday is drawing to a close, return travel flows increase across the country. (Photo by Zhao Jun/Xinhua)

item.title: Another Nanjing Massacre survivor dies, only 20 remain
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
Another survivor of the Nanjing Massacre died on Wednesday, reducing the number of registered living survivors to 20, the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders said.
Massacre survivor Guo Xiulan died at the age of 94, according to the memorial hall in Nanjing, the capital of east China's Jiangsu Province.
Guo was born in 1932. According to survivor recollections documented by the museum, when the Nanjing Massacre took place after Japanese troops captured Nanjing on December 13, 1937, Guo's parents took their three children to hide in an underground shelter along with neighbors.
"Japanese soldiers stood at the opening and strafed it with machine guns. My parents and my youngest sister perished. Only my second sister and I survived," Guo was recorded as saying.
The Nanjing Massacre unfolded over six weeks. Japanese soldiers killed approximately 300,000 Chinese civilians and unarmed soldiers in one of the most barbaric atrocities of World War II.
Over the years, the number of survivors able to share firsthand accounts of the massacre has continued to decline.
In 2014, China's top legislature designated December 13 as the national memorial day for the victims of the Nanjing Massacre. The Chinese government has also preserved survivors' testimonies through written records and video recordings.
Documents related to the massacre were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2015. To date, only 20 living survivors of the Nanjing Massacre remain on the registry maintained by the Nanjing Association for Assistance to Victims of Japanese Aggression and Inheritance of Nanjing Massacre Historical Memory.

item.title: Immersive experiences fuel inbound tourism boom over China's National Day holiday
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
Foreign tourists at the Palace Museum in Beijing, China, October 6, 2026. /VCG
China's inbound tourism market is seeing robust growth during the 2026 National Day holiday.
China's border crossings are expected to handle an average of about 2.15 million passenger trips per day during the holiday, according to the National Immigration Administration.
Data from Chinese online travel agency Trip.com showed that inbound tourist trips during the combine holiday posted double digit year-on-year growth for the first time.
New trends are emerging in China's inbound tourism market, as overseas visitors move beyond traditional sightseeing, and increasingly immerse themselves in local life, culture and experiences.
Orders for one-day inbound tours surged more than fourfold year on year, while scenic spot ticket bookings jumped over 220%. Cultural attractions accounted for around 43% of inbound scenic spot bookings during the combined holiday, up from about 32% in 2024.
Russian tourist learned black tea brewing in Huzhou, Zhejiang Province, China, June 5, 2026. /VCG
Traditional Chinese style photo shoots have also become a new source of tourism spending among foreign visitors. At Shanghai's Yu Garden, a popular destination for foreign tourists, they are dressing in traditional Chinese hanfu and taking ancient style photos against a backdrop of upturned eaves and traditional pavilions, embracing a new way to experience Eastern aesthetics.
Cultural performances are also offering foreign visitors new ways to experience and understand China. In Zhangjiajie, central China's Hunan Province, shows such as "Charming Xiangxi" blend intangible cultural heritage with real mountain and water scenery, modern lighting and multilingual subtitles. By the end of September, the "Charming Xiangxi" theater had welcomed more than 140,000 overseas visitors this year.
The "Charming Xiangxi" performance in Zhangjiajie, Hunan Province, China, October 4, 2026. /VCG
In Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, the Huaqiangbei electronics market has emerged as a popular tech shopping destination for overseas visitors, who are captivated by AI translation glasses, smartwatches, humanoid robots, portable AI speakers and panoramic cameras.
The surge in inbound tourism was fueled by China's expanding visa-free policies.
During this year's Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, from September 25 to 27, foreign nationals made 728,000 border crossings, up 37.7% year on year. Among inbound foreign visitors, a total of 247,000 entered under visa-free policies, an increase of 32.7% from a year earlier, data from the National Immigration Administration showed.
Foreign tourists arrive at Shanghai Pudong International Airport in Shanghai, China, September 30, 2026. /VCG
The growth in inbound travel is driven by the ongoing innovation in China's tourism offerings, experiences and consumption scenarios, giving international visitors more opportunities to engage with local culture and everyday life, said Li Xinjian, executive dean of the Capital Culture and Tourism Development Research Institute at Beijing International Studies University.
Li added that China is increasingly becoming a destination where travelers can not only see the sights, but also immerse themselves in the experience.

item.title: China urges France, Germany to uphold open cooperation, free trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
BEIJING, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- China hopes that France and Germany will uphold open cooperation and free trade, observe World Trade Organization rules, and refrain from encouraging the European Union (EU) to use protectionist tools at every turn, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday.
When asked to comment on media reports that France and Germany had urged the EU to make greater use of trade defense measures and roll out a number of new protectionist tools, the spokesperson said China has always maintained that interdependence is not a risk, intertwined interests do not pose a threat, and open cooperation represents the right path to development.
Protectionism cannot enhance competitiveness, and decoupling and cutting off supply chains will only harm others without benefiting oneself, the spokesperson said.
As major economies, France and Germany should not politicize trade and economic issues or overstretch the concept of national security. They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, which would ultimately backfire on themselves, the spokesperson added.

item.title: China's National Day holiday box office tops 900 million yuan
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Featuring a blend of cultural consumption and tourism, the film market during this year's week-long National Day holiday starting from October 1 has kept up a strong momentum. After a five-day streak of daily revenue reaching 100 million yuan, the total box-office earnings including advance sales for the holiday has exceeded 900 million yuan (around US$134.2 million).
Film posters are displayed at a cinema in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province on October 2, 2026. /VCG
During the holiday, a list of new domestic and foreign films hit cinemas nationwide, covering various genres such as family-friendly, animation, crime thrillers, comedy and socially themed dramas, providing a wide range of viewing options for the public.
So far, the top three films at the National Day film box office are "Traces of Justice," "Resident Evil," and "Mr. and Mrs. Pardon." The crime thriller "Traces of Justice," based on the real-life work of a forensic evidence specialist, follows investigators as they use physical evidence to solve criminal cases.
This year, the trend of film-inspired tourism continues to boom in many places across the country. For example, with the continuing popularity of the crime film "V," its shooting locations in Jiangmen, Guangdong drew many tourists to visit the iconic qilou buildings and ancient villages there. Meanwhile, a variety of cultural activities introduced across the country during the holiday also added to this trend. In Qingdao, Shandong, in addition to film-themed trains and tour routes, seaside open-air film screenings, film carnivals and cultural fairs were also organized to create new consumption scenarios for tourists.

item.title: Why the World Places Greater Trust in China?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
In this golden autumn, as heartfelt greetings of "Happy Birthday, China!" echo across continents and oceans, why does the world steadfastly choose China?
This profound trust is sparked by the spontaneous ease of "China Travel," anchored by resilient supply chains that steady the global economy, and cemented by China's commitment as a responsible major country to mutual respect and solidarity through thick and thin.
Listen to these genuine voices from around the world, and discover the true depth of this cross-continental trust!

item.title: Flag-raising ceremony held at Tian'anmen Square to celebrate 77th founding anniversary of PRC
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
A flag-raising ceremony to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China (PRC) was held at Tian'anmen Square in Beijing on Thursday.
The Guard of Honor of the Chinese People's Liberation Army escorted the national flag to the square, while the military band played the national anthem.
Many people from across China gathered at the square to watch the ceremony.

item.title: Activities held across China to celebrate National Day
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Cities across China are decorating landmark sites with national flags and floral displays as National Day arrives, and people hold various activities to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China.
